title: The Gerrymander Arms Race: Both Parties Redrew the Maps, and Voters Ignored the Lines
dek: Nine states went into the midterms with new House maps. After a special election projected at $280 million and a Supreme Court ruling, the wave washed the lines out. The problem: you shouldn't need a wave.
body:
## The map is not the territory. The voters are.

Let's talk about maps. Not the fun kind, with a dotted line to buried treasure. The other kind, drawn in a state capitol at two in the morning by people whose job, in theory, is to represent you, and whose actual hobby, it turns out, is choosing you.

Here's the scoreboard going into last Tuesday. Nine states went into the 2026 midterms with new congressional maps, and an Ohio commission, a Florida legislature, a Texas legislature, California's voters and a handful of courts all took a swing at the lines [1]. Ballotpedia's own math says those nine maps, measured against the 2024 presidential vote, were worth a net nine seats to Republicans [1]. That was the plan. Nine seats, locked in with a ruler, a spreadsheet and a press release.

Then people voted. Democrats flipped more than 40 House seats, by CBS News's count, and took the chamber [3]. By Friday, Democrats had won 253 of the 435 House seats with 27 still uncounted [9]. Which means the most sophisticated redistricting operation in modern American history accomplished roughly what a man accomplishes when he carefully rearranges the deck chairs on a ship and then the ocean votes.

So tonight: how we got a nationwide map war nobody asked for, who paid for it, why it mostly blew up in its architects' faces, and why that should not make anyone feel better.

## Everything is bigger in Texas, including the miss

This round started in Texas. In 2025, at President Trump's urging, Texas Republicans redrew the state's congressional map in the middle of the decade, aiming to turn five Democratic-held districts into seats Trump would have carried by at least 10 points, for a hoped-for 30-to-8 delegation [2]. Texas Democrats left the state to deny the legislature a quorum, which held the map up for a while, and then it passed anyway; Gov. Greg Abbott signed it on August 29, 2025 [2][1]. A three-judge federal panel blocked it that November; the Supreme Court paused that ruling three days later and let the map stand in December [1].

The point of the map, according to the Texas Tribune, was to protect the GOP's slim House majority [2]. Let's check in on how that went.

Republicans lost four of the five seats the map targeted and two of their own, and will go to Washington in January with 24 Texas seats, one fewer than they started this Congress with [2]. In the Rio Grande Valley, Democrat Bobby Pulido ousted Rep. Monica De La Cruz in a redrawn district [3]. In the 23rd, a seat that leans about 15 points toward Trump, Democrat Katy Padilla Stout won [2]. In a Houston-area district Trump won by about 20 points two years ago, Democrat Leticia Gutierrez won despite being heavily outspent [2]. Republicans did pick up exactly one Democratic seat, the 32nd [3].

There is a word for this in redistricting circles: a "dummymander," a map so greedy that it spreads its own voters too thin and hands seats to the other side when the wind turns. And Texas didn't just turn the wind. Texas built a wind tunnel, drove its own car into it, and filed a press release about the aerodynamics.

## Then everybody else wanted one

Here's the thing about an arms race: the other side gets to build arms too. Texas's redraw sparked a nationwide redistricting war that produced similarly skewed maps in other states [2].

California answered. The legislature passed a plan in August 2025, and voters approved it as Proposition 50, a constitutional amendment, that November, 65 to 35 [1]. It was designed to move five seats to Democrats [1]. That fight became one of the most expensive ballot measures in California history, with $166.2 million raised by both sides as of late October 2025 [6]. On the yes side, the biggest donors included House Majority PAC and its related committee, at $16.4 million; on the no side, a single donor, Charles T. Munger Jr., put in $32.7 million, roughly three-quarters of all the opposition money [6]. And that's just the campaigns. Running the special election itself was projected to cost more than $280 million [7]. So California's answer to "politicians are drawing districts to pick their voters" was a $280 million election to let politicians draw districts to pick their voters, but with a referendum. Which is a little like fighting a house fire by setting your own house on fire, democratically.

To be fair, it worked on its own terms: Democrats picked up all five seats they had hoped to flip, CBS reports, including the one held by Rep. David Valadao [3]. Victory. Sort of. The kind of victory where you win the fight and then look around and notice you've been fighting in a sewer.

Then the copies came. North Carolina's legislature passed a map in October 2025 aimed at one more Republican seat [1]. Ohio's redistricting commission, created by a 2018 constitutional amendment, unanimously approved a map built for two more [1]. Missouri passed one too, but a veto referendum was certified and the 2022 lines were used in November [1]; Democrat Fred Wellman then unseated Rep. Ann Wagner in the very seat Republicans had tried to make redder [3]. Florida passed a new map in April 2026 and Gov. Ron DeSantis signed it on May 4, aiming for four more Republican seats [1]. As of election night, three of the four Democratic seats it targeted had stayed blue and the fourth was within a point [2].

North Carolina, meanwhile, saw several seats change hands anyway, including the 11th District, which went Democratic for the first time since 2010 [3]. At this point the maps are less a strategy than a horoscope: vaguely confident, wildly wrong, and drawn up by someone who's never met you.

## The Supreme Court hands out more crayons

And then, this spring, the Supreme Court made the whole thing worse. On April 29, 2026, in Louisiana v. Callais, the Court ruled 6 to 3 that Louisiana's map, which had two majority-Black districts, was unconstitutional [4]. Justice Samuel Alito's majority opinion stopped short of striking down Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, but, according to the Center for American Progress, it made claims far harder to bring, including by requiring proof of intentional discrimination [5]. The Brennan Center warned the ruling would "allow racial discrimination and further encourage partisan gerrymandering" [10].

What happened next was not subtle. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry suspended the state's May 16 congressional primary, citing an "emergency," after more than 100,000 early votes had already been cast, so the legislature could redraw the map [5]. The Supreme Court then finalized its judgment immediately, skipping the usual 32-day wait [4]. In dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the ruling "has spawned chaos in the State of Louisiana" [4]. Alito, in a concurrence, said her rhetoric "lacks restraint" [4]. Which is an interesting critique of tone to deliver from inside the room that just postponed an election mid-vote.

Alabama asked the Court to bring back maps that had been struck down in Allen v. Milligan [5], and Tennessee and Louisiana passed new maps of their own in May [1]. If you voted early in Louisiana's primary, your vote was cast in an election that, functionally, got un-held. Imagine mailing in your ballot and getting a letter back that says: "Thanks! We've decided to change the question."

## Who this actually costs

Now, you might be thinking: but the voters won. The wave beat the maps. Isn't that a happy ending?

No. Because the wave is the exception, and the maps are designed for every other year. A gerrymander doesn't need to survive a hurricane. It needs to survive an ordinary Tuesday, which is most Tuesdays. And on the 2024 vote, these maps were worth nine seats to the people who drew them [1]. In a normal year, you'd never notice it working. You'd just notice your vote stopped mattering, and you'd have no idea why.

Here's who pays. Black voters in Louisiana, whose districts became a legal question and whose primary was paused in the middle of voting [5]. Californians, who got a special election projected to cost more than $280 million [7] to fix a problem their state's politicians didn't create but definitely joined. Taxpayers in states like Tennessee, which called a special session [1], so lawmakers could argue about lines instead of, say, literally anything else. And every voter in every district now drawn so that the only election that matters is the primary, where a tiny, angry slice of the electorate picks the winner.

And people hate it. In a Common Cause poll of Florida voters conducted by Noble Predictive Insights in the summer of 2025, 55 percent opposed mid-decade redistricting, including 62 percent of Democrats, 60 percent of independents, and a plurality of Republicans, 45 percent against to 36 percent for [8]. There are very few things in American life that a plurality of Florida Republicans and a majority of Florida Democrats agree on. One is that they'd prefer not to be sorted like recycling.

## The few people who said no

Credit where it's due, because it was rare. In Indiana, the House passed a new map in December 2025, and then the state Senate rejected it 31 to 19, with 21 Republicans joining Democrats [1]. In Maryland, Democrats' commission drew an all-Democratic map, and Senate President Bill Ferguson said the Senate wouldn't move forward on mid-cycle redistricting [1]. In Virginia, the legislature and voters approved a redraw, and then the state Supreme Court blocked it [1]. In Utah, a court picked a map over the legislature's, which produced one Democratic-leaning district around Salt Lake City; Democrat Ben McAdams won it [1][3].

Those are not the same thing, and some of them are messier than others. But the common thread is that somebody, somewhere, looked at the crayons and decided not to color.

## How you'd actually fix this

So what do we do? A few ideas, and these are opinions, but they're good ones.

First: ban mid-decade redraws. Once a decade, after the census, done. If your district changes every time a president gets nervous about the polls, that's not representation, that's a subscription service.

Second: take the pens away from the people being graded. Most voters already want that, if the Florida numbers are any guide [8]. And note the warning label from Ohio, whose commission was created by a reform amendment and still produced a map aimed at two more seats [1]. A reform with a politician-shaped hole in the middle is just a politician with paperwork.

Third: Congress, which now has new management [3], could set national rules instead of letting fifty legislatures run a cage match. Whether the people who just benefited from a wave will want to give up the pens is, let's say, the open question.

Because here's how this ends. This year, the voters outran the maps [3]. Good for them. But it took a wave that knocked out seats the map-makers thought were safe by 10, 15, even 20 points [2]. You shouldn't need a tsunami to get counted. You should just need a Tuesday.

pt.title: A corrida armamentista do gerrymandering: os dois partidos redesenharam os mapas, e os eleitores ignoraram as linhas
pt.dek: Nove estados chegaram às eleições de meio de mandato com novos mapas distritais. Depois de uma eleição especial estimada em US$ 280 milhões e de uma decisão da Suprema Corte, a onda apagou as linhas. O problema: ninguém deveria precisar de uma onda.

de.title: Das Gerrymandering-Wettrüsten: Beide Parteien zeichneten die Karten neu, die Wähler ignorierten die Linien
de.dek: Neun Bundesstaaten gingen mit neuen Wahlkreiskarten in die Zwischenwahlen. Nach einer auf 280 Millionen Dollar geschätzten Sonderwahl und einem Urteil des Supreme Court spülte die Welle die Linien weg. Das Problem: Man sollte keine Welle brauchen.
